(a) a compiler (b) an editor (c) an IDE (d) a debugger

(a) Compiler (b) Editor (c) IDE (d) Debugger

(a) Variables (b) Constants (c) Strings (d) Comments

Correct answer: 4

(a) -> (arrow) (b) = (assignment) (c) @ (d) ?

mcqs.why: A compiler converts the whole program file written in a high-level language into machine understandable and executable code in one go.

mcqs.why: The primitive building blocks of a language together with its grammar rules are called its syntax; every program must be written according to this syntax.

mcqs.q: A list of words that are predefined and must not be used by the programmer to name his own variables are known as _______.
mcqs.why: Reserved words have a predefined meaning in the language, so the programmer must not use them as names of his own variables.

mcqs.why: Include statements such as #include <stdio.h> are written in the header (link) section of a C program, before the main section.

mcqs.q: _______ are added in the source code to further explain the techniques and algorithms used by the programmer.
mcqs.why: Comments are added in the source code to explain the techniques and algorithms used; the compiler ignores them during execution.

mcqs.why: Constants are fixed values such as 5, 3.14 or 'A' that do not change during the whole execution of the program, unlike variables.

mcqs.why: A float variable uses 4 bytes of memory and can store a real number with up to about six digits of precision.

mcqs.why: Initialization means giving a variable its first value, and this is done with the assignment operator =, for example int age = 15;

mcqs.why: A variable is a named memory location, like a container, in which values are stored and can be changed during execution.

It combines text editor, libraries, compiler and debugger in a single interface

mcqs.q: Before a computer can execute a program written in C, the code must be:
mcqs.why: Computers understand only machine language, so the code written in the program file must be converted into machine language before it can be executed.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a reserved word in C?
mcqs.why: The book's True/False exercise confirms that 'Column' is not a reserved word of C, while int, float and return are reserved words with predefined meanings.

mcqs.q: Which software converts the whole source program into machine language in one go and produces an executable file?
mcqs.why: A compiler converts the whole source program into machine language in one go and, when the program is error-free, produces an executable file.

mcqs.why: The main section holds the main() function, and execution of a C program always starts from main(); its body is written inside curly braces { }.

lessons.title: Define the following
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) IDE

IDE stands for Integrated Development Environment. It is a software application that provides all the tools a programmer needs in one place: a text editor to write code, libraries, a compiler to convert the code into machine code, and a debugger to find and remove errors. Examples are CLion, Code::Blocks and Dev-C++.

Q: 2) Compiler

A compiler is a software that converts the whole source program written in a high-level language (such as C) into machine language in one go and produces an executable file. If there are errors in the program, the compiler reports them and the executable file is not created until the errors are removed.

Q: 3) Reserved Words

Reserved words (also called keywords) are the words that have a special, predefined meaning in a programming language, for example int, float, char, void and return in C. They are the basic building blocks of the language and cannot be used as names of variables or functions by the programmer.

Q: 4) Main section of a program

The main section of a C program is the body of the main() function, written inside curly braces { }. Execution of the program always starts from main(). All the instructions that the program has to perform are written in this section, in the order in which they are to be executed.

Q: 5) char data type

char is a data type used to store a single character, such as a letter, a digit or a symbol. A character value is written in single quotes, for example 'A' or '9'. A char variable uses 1 byte of memory and its format specifier is %c.

mcqs.q: IDE stands for:
mcqs.why: IDE stands for Integrated Development Environment, a software application that provides an editor, libraries, a compiler and a debugger in one place.

mcqs.q: A compiler, after converting an error-free program, produces:
mcqs.why: When the program is error-free, the compiler produces an executable file that can be run directly; if errors exist, it reports them and no executable file is created.

mcqs.q: Reserved words are also called:
mcqs.why: Reserved words are also called keywords; examples in C are int, float, char, void and return, and they cannot be used as variable names.

mcqs.q: A char variable uses _______ of memory.
mcqs.why: The char data type stores a single character and uses 1 byte of memory; its format specifier is %c.

mcqs.q: A character value in C is written inside:
mcqs.why: A character value is written in single quotes, for example 'A' or '9'; text in double quotes is a string, not a single character.

mcqs.q: The body of the main() function is written inside:
mcqs.why: The main section of a C program is the body of main(), written inside curly braces { }, and all instructions to be performed are written there.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of an IDE?
mcqs.why: CLion, Code::Blocks and Dev-C++ are IDEs; Notepad is only a simple text editor without compiler and debugger tools.

mcqs.q: If a program contains errors, the compiler:
options: ignores them and runs the program
reports them and does not create the executable file
mcqs.why: The compiler checks the whole program, reports the errors to the programmer, and the executable file is not created until the errors are removed.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a reserved word of C?
mcqs.why: struct is a reserved word (keyword) of C with a predefined meaning, while Column, total and marks are ordinary words that can be used as variable names.

mcqs.q: A debugger is a tool used to:
mcqs.why: An IDE includes a debugger, which is the tool used to find and remove errors (bugs) from a program.

lessons.title: Briefly answer the following questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) Why do we need a programming environment?

A programming environment (IDE) is needed because writing a program involves many steps: typing the code, saving it in a file, compiling it, and finding and correcting errors. The IDE provides an editor, compiler, libraries and a debugger together in a single interface, so all these steps can be done easily in one place without using separate programs.

Q: 2) Write the steps to create a C program file in the IDE of your lab computer.

Step 1: Open the IDE installed on the lab computer. Step 2: Click File menu and choose New / New Project (or New File) to create a new C program file. Step 3: Type the program code in the editor window. Step 4: Save the file with a suitable name and the .c extension, for example welcome.c. Step 5: Compile the program and remove any errors reported. Step 6: Run the program and see the output on the screen.

Q: 3) Describe the purpose of a compiler.

The purpose of a compiler is to convert the source code written by the programmer in a high-level language into machine language (0s and 1s), because the computer can only understand and execute machine language. The compiler checks the whole program for syntax errors, reports them to the programmer, and when the program is error-free it produces an executable file that can be run directly.

Q: 4) List down five reserved words in C programming language.

Five reserved words of C are: (1) int — used to declare integer variables. (2) float — used to declare real-number variables. (3) char — used to declare character variables. (4) void — used to show that a function returns nothing. (5) return — used to send a value back from a function. Other reserved words include if, else, for, while, break and struct.

Q: 5) Discuss the main parts of the structure of a C program.

A C program has two main parts. (1) Link / header section: it contains the include statements, for example #include <stdio.h>, which link the library files whose functions are used in the program. (2) Main section: it contains the main() function. Its body, written inside { }, holds variable declarations and all the statements that are executed when the program runs.

Q: 6) Why do we use comments in programming?

Comments are used to explain, in simple human language, what a part of the code does, so that the program becomes easy to understand for other programmers and for the programmer himself when he reads the code after a long time. Comments are ignored by the compiler and do not affect the execution or output of the program. In C, a comment is written between /* and */.

Q: 7) Differentiate between constants and variables.

A constant is a value that cannot change during the execution of the program, for example 5, 3.14 or 'A'. A variable is a named memory location (like a container) whose value can change during execution, for example in int age = 15; the variable age can be given a new value later in the program. Constants are fixed values, while variables hold values that may vary.

Q: 8) Write down the rules for naming variables.

Rules for naming a variable in C: (1) A name can contain letters, digits and underscore ( _ ) only. (2) The first character must be a letter or an underscore; it cannot be a digit. (3) No blank space or special symbol (such as @, #, %) is allowed in the name. (4) A reserved word cannot be used as a variable name. (5) C is case-sensitive, so age and Age are two different variables. Examples of valid names: total_marks, sum2. Invalid names: 2sum, my marks, float.

Q: 9) Differentiate between char and int.

int is used to store whole numbers (integers) such as 5, -12 or 100; it uses 2 bytes (in the book's compiler) and its format specifier is %d or %i. char is used to store a single character such as 'A', 'm' or '7', written in single quotes; it uses 1 byte of memory and its format specifier is %c. So the difference is in the type of data stored, the memory used and the format specifier.

Q: 10) How can we declare and initialize a variable?

Declaration means telling the compiler the name and data type of a variable, for example: int age; Initialization means giving the variable its first value at the time of declaration, using the assignment operator =, for example: int age = 15; Here age is declared as an integer variable and initialized with the value 15. In the same way, float height = 5.5; declares and initializes a float variable.

lessons.title: Match the columns
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Match column A with column B: (1) IDE, (2) Text Editor, (3) Compiler, (4) Programming Language, (5) Reserved words, (6) Link Section, (7) Body of main(), (8) Comment. Column B: (a) Machine executable code, (b) include statement, (c) Python, (d) CLion, (e) /* (a+b) */, (f) Notepad, (g) struct, (h) { }.

Correct matching: (1) IDE — (d) CLion, because CLion is an IDE used for writing C programs. (2) Text Editor — (f) Notepad, because Notepad is a simple text editor. (3) Compiler — (a) Machine executable code, because a compiler converts source code into machine executable code. (4) Programming Language — (c) Python, because Python is a programming language. (5) Reserved words — (g) struct, because struct is a reserved word of C. (6) Link Section — (b) include statement, because include statements are written in the link section. (7) Body of main() — (h) { }, because the body of main() is enclosed in curly braces. (8) Comment — (e) /* (a+b) */, because text between /* and */ is a comment.

lessons.title: Programming Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Exercise 1: Open the IDE, write the given program, save it as welcome.c and run it.

Program (as given in the book):
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
/*A simple C language program*/
printf("Welcome to C language");
getch();
}
Line-by-line explanation: Line 1 links the stdio.h library, which contains the printf function. Line 2 links conio.h, which contains getch(). Line 3 starts the main function, from where execution begins. Line 4 { opens the body of main. Line 5 is a comment; it only explains the program and is ignored by the compiler. Line 6 prints the text Welcome to C language on the screen; the semicolon ends the statement. Line 7 getch() waits for a key press so the output stays on the screen. Line 8 } closes the body of main. Output: Welcome to C language

Q: Exercise 2: Write a program that declares variables of appropriate data types to store the personal data of your best friend (initial letter of his name, initial letter of his gender, his age, his height) and initializes these variables.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
char name = 'A';
char gender = 'M';
int age = 15;
float height = 5.5;
printf("Name initial: %c ", name);
printf("Gender: %c ", gender);
printf("Age: %d ", age);
printf("Height: %f", height);
getch();
}
Explanation: A single letter (initial of name, initial of gender) is stored in a char variable, because char holds one character. Age is a whole number, so it is stored in an int variable. Height contains a decimal point (5.5 feet), so it is stored in a float variable. Each variable is initialized at the time of declaration, and printf displays the values using the format specifiers %c for char, %d for int and %f for float.

mcqs.q: In the welcome.c program, the first line #include <stdio.h> links the library that contains:
mcqs.why: The line-by-line explanation in the book states that stdio.h is linked because it contains the printf function used in the program.

mcqs.q: The getch() function used in these programs belongs to which library?
mcqs.why: The program includes conio.h because it contains the getch() function, while stdio.h contains printf.

options: a comment ignored by the compiler
mcqs.why: Text between /* and */ is a comment; it only explains the program and is ignored by the compiler.

mcqs.q: The output of the welcome.c program is:
mcqs.why: The printf statement prints the text written in double quotes, so the output is: Welcome to C language.

mcqs.q: In printf("Welcome to C language"); the semicolon at the end:
mcqs.why: The semicolon is the statement terminator; it ends the printf statement, as explained line by line in the book's solution.

mcqs.q: The initial letter of a person's name should be stored in a variable of type:
mcqs.why: A single letter is a character, and char holds one character, so the initial of the name and the initial of the gender are stored in char variables.

mcqs.q: A person's age, being a whole number, should be stored in a variable of type:
mcqs.why: Age is a whole number such as 15, so it is stored in an int variable; height 5.5 needs a float because it has a decimal point.

mcqs.q: A height of 5.5 feet should be stored in a variable of type:
mcqs.why: Height contains a decimal point (5.5), so it must be stored in a float variable; an int would cut off the fractional part.

mcqs.q: In the friend-data program, the height is printed with the format specifier:
mcqs.why: The solution uses %c for char values, %d for the int age and %f for the float height in the printf statements.

mcqs.q: In these programs, getch() at the end is used to:
options: convert the program to machine code
wait for a key press so the output stays on the screen
mcqs.why: As the book explains, getch() waits for a key press so that the output stays on the screen for the user to see.

lessons.title: Multiple Choice Questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: printf is used to print _______ type of data.

(a) int (b) float (c) char (d) All of them
Correct answer: All of them

Q: scanf is a _______ in C programming language.

(a) Keyword (b) library (c) function (d) none of them
Correct answer: function

Q: getch() is used to take _______ as input from user.

(a) int (b) float (c) char (d) All of them
Correct answer: char

Q: In the code: int a = 4; float b = 2.2; a = a * b; what will be the value of variable a after execution?

(a) 8.8 (b) 8 (c) 8.0 (d) 8.2
Correct answer: 8

Q: Which of the following is a valid line of code?

(a) int = 20; (b) grade = 'A'; (c) line = this is a line; (d) none of them
Correct answer: grade = 'A';

Q: Which operator has highest precedence among the following?

(a) / (division) (b) = (assignment) (c) > (greater than) (d) ! (NOT)
Correct answer: ! (NOT)

Q: Which of the following is not a type of operator?

(a) Arithmetic operator (b) Check operator (c) Relational operator (d) Logical operator
Correct answer: Check operator

Q: The operator % is used to calculate _______.

(a) Percentage (b) Remainder (c) Factorial (d) Square
Correct answer: Remainder

Q: Which of the following is a valid character?

(a) 'here' (b) "a" (double quotes) (c) '9' (d) None of them
Correct answer: '9'

Q: What is true about C language?

(a) C is not a case sensitive language (b) Keywords can be used as variable names (c) All logical operators are binary operators (d) None of them
Correct answer: None of them

mcqs.q: printf is used to print _______ type of data.
mcqs.why: With the proper format specifiers, printf can print every type of data: %d for int, %f for float and %c for char, so it prints int, float and char data.

mcqs.q: scanf is a _______ in C programming language.
mcqs.why: scanf is a built-in library function of C (available in stdio.h) used to take input from the user; it is not a keyword.

mcqs.q: getch() is used to take _______ as input from user.
mcqs.why: getch() takes only a single character as input; unlike scanf it cannot take int or float data.

mcqs.q: In the code: int a = 4; float b = 2.2; a = a * b; what will be the value of variable a after execution?
mcqs.why: Working: a * b = 4 x 2.2 = 8.8. But a is an int variable, so the fractional part is removed when the result is stored, and a becomes 8.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a valid line of code?
mcqs.why: grade = 'A'; correctly assigns a character written in single quotes to a variable. 'int = 20;' uses a reserved word as a variable name, and a line of text cannot be assigned without quotes.

mcqs.q: Which operator has highest precedence among the following?
mcqs.why: The NOT operator ! is a unary operator, and unary operators have higher precedence than division, relational and assignment operators.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is not a type of operator?
mcqs.why: C has arithmetic, relational and logical operators (and others such as assignment), but there is no operator type called a Check operator.

mcqs.q: The operator % is used to calculate _______.
mcqs.why: The % operator is the modulus operator; it gives the remainder after division, for example 17 % 5 = 2.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a valid character?
mcqs.why: A character is a single symbol written in single quotes, so '9' is a valid character. 'here' has more than one character and "a" in double quotes is a string.

mcqs.q: Which of the following statements about C language is TRUE?
options: C is not a case sensitive language
Keywords can be used as variable names
All logical operators are binary operators
mcqs.why: C is case-sensitive (age and Age are different variables). Keywords cannot be used as variable names, and the logical operator ! (NOT) is unary, so the other three statements are false.

Answer: False

Q: Format specifiers begin with a % sign.

Answer: True

Q: Precedence of division operator is greater than multiplication operator.

mcqs.q: Format specifiers in C begin with which sign?
mcqs.why: Every format specifier begins with the % sign, for example %d, %f and %c, as the book states in the definition of a format specifier.

mcqs.q: The precedence of the division operator compared to the multiplication operator is:
options: equal - both are evaluated left to right
mcqs.why: The book's True/False exercise marks 'precedence of division is greater than multiplication' as False: * and / have equal precedence and are evaluated from left to right.

mcqs.q: getch() can take which type of input from the user?

mcqs.q: scanf is used for which operation?
mcqs.why: The statement 'scanf is used for output operations' is False: scanf is the input function, while printf is used for output operations.

mcqs.q: Which pair of functions is correctly matched with its work?

lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) Statement Terminator

The statement terminator is the semicolon ( ; ) used at the end of every statement in C. It tells the compiler that the statement has finished and the next statement begins after it. If the semicolon is missed, the compiler gives a syntax error.

Q: 2) Format Specifier

A format specifier is a special code used inside printf and scanf to tell the type of data being printed or read. Every format specifier begins with the % sign, for example %d or %i for integer, %f for float and %c for character.

Q: 3) Escape Sequence

An escape sequence is a combination of characters that starts with a backslash ( \ ) and has a special meaning inside a string. It is used to print something that cannot be typed directly. Examples: \n takes the cursor to a new line and \t gives a tab space.

Q: 4) scanf

scanf is a built-in input function of C (available in stdio.h) used to take input from the user through the keyboard and store it in a variable. Its general form is: scanf("%d", &a); where %d is the format specifier for the type of data and &a gives the address of the variable a in memory.

Q: 5) Modulus Operator

The modulus operator ( % ) is an arithmetic operator that gives the remainder after division of two integers. For example, 17 % 5 = 2, because 17 divided by 5 leaves remainder 2. It is commonly used to check whether a number is even or odd and to extract digits of a number.

lessons.title: Briefly answer the following questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) What is the difference between scanf and getch?

scanf is an input function that can take all types of data (int, float, char etc.) from the user; the user types the value and presses Enter, and the value is stored in a variable using its address, for example scanf("%d", &a);. getch() takes only a single character as input; it does not show (echo) the character on the screen and does not wait for the Enter key. scanf is used for proper data input, while getch() is mostly used to hold the output screen or read one character.

Q: 2) Which function of C language is used to display output on screen?

The printf() function is used to display output on the screen. It is a built-in function of the stdio.h library. Text written in double quotes is printed as it is, and values of variables are printed by using format specifiers, for example printf("Sum = %d", sum); prints the value of the variable sum.

Q: 3) Why format specifiers are important to be specified in I/O operations?

Format specifiers are important because they tell the printf and scanf functions what type of data is being handled — integer, float or character. Each type occupies a different amount of memory and is stored in a different format. If the correct format specifier is not used, the function cannot read or print the value correctly and the program gives a wrong result or garbage value. For example, %d must be used for an int, %f for a float and %c for a char.

Q: 4) What are escape sequences? Why do we need them?

Escape sequences are character combinations that begin with a backslash ( \ ) and represent a special action inside a string, for example \n for new line and \t for tab space. We need them because some things cannot be typed directly inside a string: we cannot press Enter in the middle of a string to change the line, and we cannot easily give a wide tab gap. Escape sequences make the output properly formatted and readable.

Q: 5) Which operators are used for arithmetic operations?

The arithmetic operators of C are: + for addition, - for subtraction, * for multiplication, / for division and % (modulus) for remainder after division. For example, if a = 17 and b = 5, then a + b = 22, a - b = 12, a * b = 85, a / b = 3 (integer division) and a % b = 2.

Q: 6) What are relational operators? Describe with an example.

Relational operators are used to compare two values. The result of a comparison is either 1 (condition satisfied) or 0 (condition not satisfied). The relational operators are: < less than, > greater than, <= less than or equal to, >= greater than or equal to, == equal to, and != not equal to. Example: if a = 8 and b = 5, then a > b gives 1, a == b gives 0 and a != b gives 1.

Q: 7) What are logical operators? Describe with an example.

Logical operators are used to combine two or more conditions into one condition. There are three logical operators: && (AND) — the combined condition is satisfied only when all conditions are satisfied; || (OR) — satisfied when at least one condition is satisfied; ! (NOT) — reverses the result of a condition. Example: (marks >= 40 && attendance >= 75) is satisfied only when a student both passes and has enough attendance.

Q: 8) What is the difference between unary operators and binary operators?

A unary operator works on only one operand, for example ++ (increment), -- (decrement) and ! (NOT): in a++ only one variable a is involved. A binary operator works on two operands, for example +, -, *, /, % and ==: in a + b, two operands a and b are involved. So the difference is the number of operands the operator acts upon.

Q: 9) What is the difference between == operator and = operator?

The = operator is the assignment operator; it stores the value written on its right side into the variable on its left side, for example a = 5; stores 5 in a. The == operator is the relational (equal to) operator; it compares two values and gives 1 if they are equal and 0 if they are not, for example a == 5 checks whether a is equal to 5. Writing = in place of == in a condition is a common logical error.

Q: 10) What is meant by precedence of operators? Which operator has the highest precedence in C language?

Precedence of operators means the order or priority in which operators are evaluated in an expression when more than one operator is present. The operator with higher precedence is evaluated first, just as multiplication is done before addition in mathematics. In C, parentheses ( ) have the highest precedence, followed by unary operators such as !, ++ and --; among arithmetic operators, *, / and % have higher precedence than + and -. For example, in 2 + 3 * 4, the multiplication is done first, so the result is 14, not 20.

It displays the typed character on the screen
It waits for the Enter key
It takes a single character without showing it on the screen
mcqs.why: getch() takes only a single character, does not echo (show) it on the screen and does not wait for the Enter key, unlike scanf which takes all types of data.

mcqs.q: Which function of C is used to display output on the screen?
mcqs.why: The printf() function of the stdio.h library displays output on the screen; values of variables are printed with format specifiers.

mcqs.q: If a wrong format specifier is used in an I/O operation, the result is:
options: the program prints the specifier itself
a wrong result or a garbage value
mcqs.why: Each data type is stored in a different format, so with a wrong format specifier the function cannot read or print the value correctly and gives a wrong result or garbage value.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT an arithmetic operator?
mcqs.why: The arithmetic operators are +, -, *, / and %. The == operator is a relational operator used to compare two values.

mcqs.q: If a = 17 and b = 5, then a / b in C gives:
mcqs.why: Working: both a and b are integers, so integer division is performed: 17 / 5 = 3 (the fractional part is discarded), while a % b = 2.

mcqs.q: The result of a relational operation in C is:
options: 1 if the condition is satisfied, 0 if not
the sum of the two values
mcqs.why: Relational operators compare two values and the result is 1 when the condition is satisfied and 0 when it is not satisfied.

mcqs.q: If a = 8 and b = 5, then the value of a == b is:
mcqs.why: Working: a == b compares 8 with 5; they are not equal, so the condition is not satisfied and the result is 0. (a > b would give 1 and a != b would give 1.)

mcqs.q: The combined condition with the AND operator (&&) is satisfied only when:
options: at least one condition is satisfied
mcqs.why: With && (AND), the combined condition is satisfied only when all the joined conditions are satisfied; with || (OR), at least one is enough.

mcqs.q: The logical NOT operator (!) works on how many operands?
mcqs.why: ! (NOT) is a unary operator: it works on only one operand and reverses its result, unlike && and || which are binary operators.

mcqs.q: The ++ and -- operators are examples of:
mcqs.why: ++ (increment) and -- (decrement) act on only one operand, for example a++, so they are unary operators; +, % and == act on two operands.

mcqs.q: The = operator in C is used to:
options: store a value into a variable
mcqs.why: = is the assignment operator: a = 5; stores 5 in a. Comparing for equality is done with ==, and confusing the two is a common logical error.

mcqs.q: The value of the expression 2 + 3 * 4 is:
mcqs.why: Working: multiplication has higher precedence than addition, so 3 * 4 = 12 is calculated first, and then 2 + 12 = 14, not 20.

mcqs.q: Which has the highest precedence in C?
mcqs.why: Parentheses ( ) have the highest precedence in C, followed by unary operators; among arithmetic operators, *, / and % come before + and -.

mcqs.q: The operators *, / and % have _______ precedence than + and -.
mcqs.why: In an expression, *, / and % are evaluated before + and - because they have higher precedence, just as multiplication is done before addition in mathematics.

mcqs.q: Which of the following operators is a binary operator?
mcqs.why: The % operator works on two operands, as in a % b, so it is a binary operator; !, ++ and -- work on a single operand and are unary.

lessons.title: Write down output of the following code segments
lessons.notes_html:
Q: a) int x = 2, y = 3, z = 6; int ans1, ans2, ans3; ans1 = x / z * y; ans2 = y + z / y * 2; ans3 = z / x + x * y; printf("%d %d %d", ans1, ans2, ans3);

Working: ans1 = x / z * y = 2 / 6 * 3. Integer division 2 / 6 gives 0, so ans1 = 0 * 3 = 0. ans2 = y + z / y * 2 = 3 + 6 / 3 * 2. Division and multiplication are done first from left to right: 6 / 3 = 2, 2 * 2 = 4, so ans2 = 3 + 4 = 7. ans3 = z / x + x * y = 6 / 2 + 2 * 3 = 3 + 6 = 9. Output: 0 7 9

Q: b) printf("nn nnn n t "); printf("nn /n/n nn/n ");

Working: In the first printf, the ordinary letters are printed as they are, moves the cursor to a new line and gives a tab space; /n without a backslash is printed as ordinary characters. Output:
nn
(blank line)
nnn
n
t (followed by two tab spaces)
nn /n/n nn/n
In words: the first line shows nn, the second line is blank, the third line shows nnn, the fourth line shows n, the fifth line shows t with tab gaps, and the last line shows the text nn /n/n nn/n because those slashes have no backslash before them.

Q: c) int a = 4, b; float c = 2.3; b = c * a; printf("%d", b);

Working: c * a = 2.3 * 4 = 9.2. This result is stored in b, which is an int variable, so the fractional part .2 is removed (truncated) and only 9 is stored. Output: 9

Q: d) int a = 4 * 3 / (5 + 1) + 7 % 4; printf("%d", a);

Working: Parentheses are solved first: (5 + 1) = 6. Then multiplication, division and modulus from left to right: 4 * 3 = 12; 12 / 6 = 2; 7 % 4 = 3 (remainder). Then addition: 2 + 3 = 5. Output: 5

Q: e) printf("%d", (((5 > 3) && (4 > 6)) || (7 > 3)));

Working: (5 > 3) is satisfied, value 1. (4 > 6) is not satisfied, value 0. So (1 && 0) gives 0, because AND needs both sides satisfied. (7 > 3) is satisfied, value 1. Then (0 || 1) gives 1, because OR is satisfied when at least one side is satisfied. Output: 1

mcqs.why: Working: ans1 = 2 / 6 * 3. Integer division 2 / 6 gives 0, so ans1 = 0 * 3 = 0.

mcqs.q: In segment (a), the value of ans2 = y + z / y * 2 is:
mcqs.why: Working: division and multiplication are done first from left to right: 6 / 3 = 2 and 2 * 2 = 4, so ans2 = 3 + 4 = 7.

mcqs.q: In segment (a), the value of ans3 = z / x + x * y is:
mcqs.why: Working: ans3 = 6 / 2 + 2 * 3 = 3 + 6 = 9, because division and multiplication are evaluated before addition.

mcqs.q: In segment (b), the text /n written without a backslash is printed as:
mcqs.why: Only \n with a backslash is an escape sequence; /n without a backslash has no special meaning and is printed as the ordinary characters /n.

mcqs.q: In segment (b), the escape sequence \t produces:
mcqs.why: In the first printf of segment (b), \n moves the cursor to a new line and \t gives a tab space, as shown in the book's working.

mcqs.q: In segment (c) — float c = 2.3; int b; b = c * a with a = 4; — the output printed for b is:
mcqs.why: Working: c * a = 2.3 * 4 = 9.2, but b is an int variable, so the fractional part .2 is removed (truncated) and only 9 is stored and printed.

mcqs.q: In segment (c), the value 9.2 becomes 9 because:
options: b is an int variable, so the fractional part is truncated
mcqs.why: Storing a float result in an int variable removes the fractional part; 9.2 is truncated to 9, not rounded.

mcqs.q: In segment (d) — int a = 4 * 3 / (5 + 1) + 7 % 4; — the value of 7 % 4 is:
mcqs.why: Working: 7 % 4 gives the remainder when 7 is divided by 4, which is 3; this value is added in the expression for a.

mcqs.q: The output of segment (d) is:
mcqs.why: Working: parentheses first: (5 + 1) = 6. Then 4 * 3 = 12, 12 / 6 = 2 and 7 % 4 = 3. Finally a = 2 + 3 = 5.

mcqs.q: The output of segment (e) — printf("%d", (((5 > 3) && (4 > 6)) || (7 > 3))); — is:
mcqs.why: Working: (5 > 3) = 1 and (4 > 6) = 0, so (1 && 0) = 0. (7 > 3) = 1, and (0 || 1) = 1 because OR needs only one side satisfied. Output: 1.

lessons.title: Identify errors in the following code segments
lessons.notes_html:
Q: a) void main() { int a, b = 13; b = a % 2; printf("Value of b is : %d, b); }

Errors: (1) The variable a is used in b = a % 2 without being given any value first, so it contains a garbage value and the result is meaningless; a must be initialized, for example int a = 10, b = 13;. (2) The closing quotation mark is placed wrongly in printf: "Value of b is : %d, b) — the format string must close before the variable, like this: printf("Value of b is : %d", b);

Q: b) void main() { int a, b, c, printf("Enter First Number: "); scanf("%d", &a); printf("Enter second number : "); scanf("%d", &b); a + b = c; ]

Errors: (1) The declaration int a, b, c, ends with a comma; it must end with a semicolon: int a, b, c;. (2) The statement a + b = c; is wrong, because a value can only be assigned to a variable, not to an expression; it must be written as c = a + b;. (3) The body of main is closed with ] instead of }. Corrected ending: c = a + b; printf("%d", c); }

Q: c) #include<stdio.h>; main() { int num; printf(Enter number: "); scanf(%d, &num); }; and the segment: include<stdio.h> int main() { float f; printf["Enter value: "]; scanf("%c", &f); }

Errors in the first segment: (1) A semicolon is written after #include<stdio.h> — an include statement never ends with a semicolon. (2) main() is written without a return type; it should be int main() or void main(). (3) The opening quotation mark is missing in printf(Enter number: ") — it must be printf("Enter number: ");. (4) The format specifier in scanf is written without quotes: scanf(%d, &num) must be scanf("%d", &num);. (5) The extra }; at the end is wrong; the function body closes with } only. Errors in the second segment: (6) # is missing before include. (7) printf is used with square brackets printf[ ] instead of parentheses printf( ). (8) A float value is read with %c, which is for characters; it must be %f: scanf("%f", &f);

mcqs.q: In segment (a), the variable a is used in b = a % 2 without being given a value first. Such a variable contains:
mcqs.why: A declared but uninitialized variable holds a garbage value, so b = a % 2 gives a meaningless result; a must be initialized first, for example int a = 10.

mcqs.q: In segment (a), the error in printf("Value of b is : %d, b); is:
options: the closing quotation mark is placed wrongly
mcqs.why: The format string must close before the variable: printf("Value of b is : %d", b); In the segment, the closing quote is placed after b, inside the string.

mcqs.q: In segment (b), the declaration int a, b, c, is wrong because it ends with:
options: a comma instead of a semicolon
mcqs.why: A declaration statement must end with a semicolon: int a, b, c; Ending it with a comma is a syntax error.

mcqs.q: The statement a + b = c; in segment (b) is wrong because:
options: addition is not allowed in C
a value can only be assigned to a variable, not to an expression
b cannot be added to a
mcqs.why: Assignment stores a value into a variable, so the statement must be written as c = a + b; The expression a + b cannot receive a value.

mcqs.q: In segment (b), the body of main is closed with the symbol ] . It must be closed with:
mcqs.why: The body of a function is enclosed in curly braces and must be closed with }; closing it with ] is an error.

mcqs.q: In segment (c), a semicolon is written after #include<stdio.h>. This is an error because:
options: include statements are written at the end
an include statement never ends with a semicolon
semicolons are not used in C
mcqs.why: The #include line only links a library file; it is not a statement, so it never ends with a semicolon.

mcqs.q: In segment (c), main() is written without a return type. It should be written as:
mcqs.why: Every function definition needs a return type; main should be written as int main() or void main().

mcqs.q: The error in scanf(%d, &num); in segment (c) is:
options: the format specifier is written without quotes
mcqs.why: The format specifier is a string and must be written in double quotes: scanf("%d", &num);

mcqs.q: In the second part of segment (c), printf["Enter value: "] is wrong because printf is used with:
mcqs.why: A function is called with parentheses ( ), so it must be printf("Enter value: "); square brackets [ ] are used for arrays, not for calling functions.

mcqs.q: In the second part of segment (c), a float value f is read with scanf("%c", &f);. The correct specifier is:
mcqs.why: %c is for characters; a float value must be read with %f, so the statement should be scanf("%f", &f);

lessons.title: Programming Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Exercise 1: Wages of an employee. Basic Salary = Pay Rate Per Hour x Working Hours; Overtime Salary = Overtime Pay Rate x Overtime Hours; Total Salary = Basic Salary + Overtime Salary. Write a program that takes working hours and overtime hours of an employee as input and displays the total salary.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
float rate, orate, basic, overtime, total;
int hours, ohours;
printf("Enter pay rate per hour: ");
scanf("%f", &rate);
printf("Enter working hours: ");
scanf("%d", &hours);
printf("Enter overtime pay rate: ");
scanf("%f", &orate);
printf("Enter overtime hours: ");
scanf("%d", &ohours);
basic = rate * hours;
overtime = orate * ohours;
total = basic + overtime;
printf("Total Salary = %f", total);
getch();
}
Explanation: The program first reads the pay rate per hour, the normal working hours, the overtime pay rate and the overtime hours from the user with scanf. It then applies the given formulas: basic salary is rate multiplied by working hours, overtime salary is overtime rate multiplied by overtime hours, and the total salary is the sum of the two. In the end printf displays the total salary.

Q: Exercise 2: Write a program that takes Celsius temperature as input, converts it into Fahrenheit (F = 9/5 C + 32) and shows the output.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
float c, f;
printf("Enter temperature in Celsius: ");
scanf("%f", &c);
f = 9.0 / 5 * c + 32;
printf("Temperature in Fahrenheit = %f", f);
getch();
}
Explanation: The temperature in Celsius is stored in the float variable c. The formula F = 9/5 x C + 32 is applied. Here 9.0 / 5 is written with a decimal point so that the division gives 1.8 and not 1 (integer division would spoil the result). The converted value is stored in f and displayed. Example: for C = 100, F = 1.8 x 100 + 32 = 212.

Q: Exercise 3: Write a program that displays the output ( * * * * on the first line and 1 2 3 4 on the second line) using a single printf statement.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
printf("* * * * 1 2 3 4");
getch();
}
Explanation: Only one printf statement is used, as required. The escape sequence inside the string ends the first line and takes the cursor to the second line, so the numbers 1 2 3 4 are printed below the stars. Spaces inside the string give the gaps between the stars and the numbers.

Q: Exercise 4: Write a program that displays the output (I am a Boy / I live in Pakistan / I am a proud Pakistani, each on a separate line) using a single printf statement.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
printf("I am a Boy I live in Pakistan I am a proud Pakistani");
getch();
}
Explanation: A single printf prints all three lines. After each line, the escape sequence moves the cursor to the beginning of the next line, so the three sentences appear one below the other exactly as required.

Q: Exercise 5: A clothing brand offers 15% discount on each item. A lady buys 5 shirts (423, 320, 270, 680, 520). Write a program that calculates the total price after discount and the amount of discount availed. Use 5 variables to store the prices.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int s1 = 423, s2 = 320, s3 = 270, s4 = 680, s5 = 520;
float total, discount, payable;
total = s1 + s2 + s3 + s4 + s5;
discount = total * 15 / 100;
payable = total - discount;
printf("Total price = %f ", total);
printf("Discount = %f ", discount);
printf("Price after discount = %f", payable);
getch();
}
Explanation: The five prices are stored in five separate variables s1 to s5, as instructed. Their sum is 423 + 320 + 270 + 680 + 520 = 2213, stored in total. The discount is 15% of the total: 2213 x 15 / 100 = 331.95. The payable price is 2213 - 331.95 = 1881.05. All three values are displayed.

Q: Exercise 6: Write a program that swaps the values of two integer variables without the help of any third variable.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int a, b;
printf("Enter two numbers: ");
scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);
a = a + b;
b = a - b;
a = a - b;
printf("After swapping: a = %d, b = %d", a, b);
getch();
}
Explanation: No third variable is used. Suppose a = 4 and b = 7. The statement a = a + b makes a = 11 (the sum holds both values). Then b = a - b gives b = 11 - 7 = 4, which is the old value of a. Then a = a - b gives a = 11 - 4 = 7, which is the old value of b. The values are swapped.

Q: Exercise 7: Write a program that takes a 5-digit number as input, and calculates and displays the sum of the first and last digit of the number.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int n, first, last, sum;
printf("Enter a 5-digit number: ");
scanf("%d", &n);
last = n % 10;
first = n / 10000;
sum = first + last;
printf("Sum of first and last digit = %d", sum);
getch();
}
Explanation: The last digit is obtained with the modulus operator: n % 10 gives the remainder when n is divided by 10, which is its last digit. The first digit of a 5-digit number is obtained by integer division n / 10000, which removes the last four digits. Example: for n = 25341, last = 1 and first = 2, so the sum displayed is 3.

Q: Exercise 8: Write a program that takes monthly income and monthly expenses (electricity bill, gas bill, food expense) of the user. The program should calculate total monthly expenses, total yearly expenses, monthly savings, yearly saving, average saving per month and average expense per month.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
float income, elec, gas, food;
float mExp, yExp, mSave, ySave, avgSave, avgExp;
printf("Enter monthly income: ");
scanf("%f", &income);
printf("Enter electricity bill, gas bill, food expense: ");
scanf("%f %f %f", &elec, &gas, &food);
mExp = elec + gas + food;
yExp = mExp * 12;
mSave = income - mExp;
ySave = mSave * 12;
avgSave = ySave / 12;
avgExp = yExp / 12;
printf("Total monthly expenses = %f ", mExp);
printf("Total yearly expenses = %f ", yExp);
printf("Monthly savings = %f ", mSave);
printf("Yearly saving = %f ", ySave);
printf("Average saving per month = %f ", avgSave);

printf("Enter steps: ");

#include <conio.h>

lessons.title: Define the following
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) Control Statements

Control statements are the statements that control the flow of execution of a program, that is, they describe the sequence in which the statements of the program are executed. Instead of always running line by line, the program can take decisions and repeat work with the help of control statements.

Q: 2) Selection Statements

Selection statements are control statements that select one set of instructions to execute from two or more options, depending on whether a condition is satisfied or not. The if statement and the if-else statement are selection statements. They are used to make decisions in a program.

Q: 3) Sequential Control

Sequential control is the normal flow of a program in which statements are executed one after another, in the same order in which they are written, from top to bottom, without skipping any statement and without repeating any statement. It is the default way of execution when no selection or loop statement is used.

Q: 4) Condition

A condition is an expression that is checked to make a decision. It gives only one of two results: satisfied (value 1) or not satisfied (value 0). A condition can be an arithmetic, relational or logical expression, for example marks >= 40. Selection statements execute their statements only when the condition is satisfied.

Q: 5) Nested Selection Structures

Nested selection structures are selection statements written inside other selection statements, that is, an if or if-else inside the body of another if or if-else. They are used when a second decision has to be taken after the first decision, for example checking the grade of a student only after checking that he has passed.

lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) Why do we need selection statements?

We need selection statements because in real life a program does not always have to do the same work; it has to take decisions according to the situation. For example, a result program prints Pass for one student and Fail for another. Selection statements (if and if-else) allow the program to test a condition and execute different instructions for different situations. Without them, every statement would run in the same fixed order for every input.

Q: 2) Differentiate between sequential and selection statements.

In sequential execution, statements run one after another in the order they are written; every statement is executed exactly once and no decision is taken. In selection statements, a condition is tested first, and only the statements of the selected part are executed while the other part is skipped. Example: in sequential flow both lines printf("Pass"); and printf("Fail"); would always run, but with if-else only one of them runs, depending on the marks.

Q: 3) Differentiate between if statement and if-else statement with an example.

The if statement has only one block: its statements execute when the condition is satisfied, and if the condition is not satisfied nothing happens and the program simply moves ahead. The if-else statement has two blocks: the if block executes when the condition is satisfied and the else block executes when it is not satisfied, so one of the two blocks always runs. Example: if (age >= 18) printf("Adult"); prints Adult only for age 18 or more. With if-else: if (age >= 18) printf("Adult"); else printf("Minor"); prints Adult or Minor — one message in every case.

Q: 4) What is the use of nested selection structures?

Nested selection structures are used when a decision depends on another decision, that is, a second condition has to be checked only after the first condition has been satisfied (or not satisfied). For example, a university first checks whether a student has passed the entry test; only then it checks his marks to decide the department. Such multi-level decisions cannot be written with a single if, so an if is placed inside another if.

Q: 5) Write the structure of if statement with brief description.

Structure of the if statement:
if (condition)
{
statements;
}
Description: The keyword if is followed by a condition written in parentheses ( ). If the condition is satisfied (non-zero), the statements written inside the block { } are executed. If the condition is not satisfied (zero), the block is skipped and the program continues with the statement written after the block. When the block has only one statement, the braces may be omitted.

lessons.title: Identify errors in the following code segments (variables are already declared)
lessons.notes_html:
Q: a) if (x ≥ 10) printf("Good");

Error: The symbol used in the condition is the mathematical symbol, which is not a C operator; the compiler cannot understand it. In C, greater than or equal to is written with two characters as >=. Corrected code: if (x >= 10) printf("Good");

Q: b) if (a < b && b < c); sum = a + b + c; else multiply = a * b * c;

Error: A semicolon is written immediately after the if condition. This semicolon becomes an empty statement belonging to the if, so the if ends there and the following else has no matching if, which is a compile-time error. Corrected code: if (a < b && b < c) sum = a + b + c; else multiply = a * b * c; (remove the semicolon after the condition).

Q: c) if (a < 7 < b) printf("7");

Error: Two comparisons are chained together in one condition, which is not allowed in C. The expression a < 7 < b is evaluated as (a < 7) < b, that is, the result 1 or 0 is compared with b, which is not the intended meaning. To check that 7 lies between a and b, the two comparisons must be joined with the AND operator: if (a < 7 && 7 < b) printf("7");

Q: d) if (a == b &| x == y) flag = true; else flag = false;

Error: The operator &| does not exist in C. A single & is the bitwise AND operator, while the logical OR operator is written as || (two vertical bars). Corrected code: if (a == b || x == y) flag = true; else flag = false;

Q: e) if (sum == 60 || product == 175) printf("Accepted %c", sum); else if (sum >= 45 || product > 100) printf("Considered %d" + sum); else printf("Rejected");

Errors: (1) In the first printf, the format specifier %c is used for sum, which is an integer value; %c would print a character, so it must be %d: printf("Accepted %d", sum);. (2) In the second printf, the variable sum is added to the string with + : printf("Considered %d" + sum); — a value cannot be added to a string in C. The variable must be passed after the string, separated by a comma: printf("Considered %d", sum);

lessons.title: Write down output of the following code segments
lessons.notes_html:
Q: a) int a = 7, b = 10; a = a + b; if (a > 20 && b < 20) b = a + b; printf("a = %d, b = %d", a, b);

Working: a = a + b = 7 + 10 = 17. The condition (a > 20 && b < 20) becomes (17 > 20 && 10 < 20). The first part is not satisfied, so the AND condition fails and b is not changed; b remains 10. Output: a = 17, b = 10

Q: b) int x = 45; if (x + 20 * 7 == 455) printf("Look's Good"); else printf("Hope for the Best");

Working: Multiplication is done before addition, so x + 20 * 7 = 45 + 140 = 185. The condition 185 == 455 is not satisfied, so the else part executes. Output: Hope for the Best

Q: c) char c1 = 'Y', c2 = 'N'; int n1 = 5, n2 = 9; n1 = n1 + 1; c1 = c2; if (n1 == n2 && c1 == c2) printf("%d = %d and %c = %c", n1, n2, c1, c1); else if (n1 < n2 && c1 == c2) printf("%d < %d and %c = %c", n1, n2, c1, c2); else printf("Better Luck Next Time!");

Working: n1 becomes 5 + 1 = 6, and c1 = c2 makes c1 = 'N', so now c1 and c2 are equal. First condition: (n1 == n2) is (6 == 9), not satisfied, so the AND fails. The else-if condition: (n1 < n2 && c1 == c2) is (6 < 9 and 'N' == 'N'), both satisfied, so the second printf executes. Output: 6 < 9 and N = N

Q: d) int a = 34, b = 32, c = 7, d = 15; a = b + c + d; if (a < 100) a = a * 2; b = b * c; c = c + d; if (a > b && c == d) { c = d; b = c; a = b; } else if (a > b && c > d || b >= d + c) { d = c * c; a = b * b; } printf("a=%d, b=%d, c=%d, d=%d", a, b, c, d);

Working step by step: a = 32 + 7 + 15 = 54. Since 54 < 100, a = 54 * 2 = 108. b = 32 * 7 = 224. c = 7 + 15 = 22. Outer condition (a > b && c == d) = (108 > 224 ...) is not satisfied, so the else part is checked: (a > b && c > d || b >= d + c). The AND part is not satisfied, but (b >= d + c) = (224 >= 15 + 22 = 37) is satisfied, and OR needs only one side, so the block runs: d = c * c = 22 * 22 = 484, and a = b * b = 224 * 224 = 50176. Output: a=50176, b=224, c=22, d=484

Q: e) int x = 5, y = 7, z = 9; if (x % 2 == 0) x++; else x = y + z; printf("x = %d\n", x); if (x % 2 == 1 && y % 2 == 1 && z % 2 == 1) printf("All are Odd"); if (x > y || x < z) { if (x > y) y++; else if (x < z) x++; } printf("x = %d, y = %d, z = %d", x, y, z);

Working step by step: x % 2 = 5 % 2 = 1, which is not equal to 0, so the else part runs: x = y + z = 7 + 9 = 16. The first printf prints x = 16. Next condition needs x % 2 == 1, but 16 % 2 = 0, so All are Odd is not printed. Next, (x > y || x < z) = (16 > 7) is satisfied, so the outer block runs; inside it (x > y) is satisfied, so y++ makes y = 8. Final output: x = 16 (on the first line), then x = 16, y = 8, z = 9

Q: Exercise 1: Write a program that takes two integers as input and tells whether the first one is a factor of the second one.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int a, b;
printf("Enter first number: ");
scanf("%d", &a);
printf("Enter second number: ");
scanf("%d", &b);
if (b % a == 0)
printf("%d is a factor of %d", a, b);
else
printf("%d is not a factor of %d", a, b);
getch();
}
Explanation: A number a is a factor of b if b divided by a leaves no remainder. The modulus operator gives the remainder: b % a. If the remainder is 0, the if block prints that a is a factor of b; otherwise the else block prints that it is not. Example: for a = 4 and b = 20, 20 % 4 = 0, so 4 is a factor of 20.

Q: Exercise 2: Write a program that takes a number as input and displays YES if the input number is a multiple of 3 and has 5 in its unit's place, e.g. 15, 75.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int n;
printf("Enter a number: ");
scanf("%d", &n);
if (n % 3 == 0 && n % 10 == 5)
printf("YES");
else
printf("NO");
getch();
}
Explanation: Two conditions must hold together, so they are joined with the AND operator &&. The first condition n % 3 == 0 checks that the number is a multiple of 3. The second condition n % 10 == 5 extracts the unit (last) digit with the modulus operator and checks that it is 5. Only when both are satisfied, YES is displayed. Example: 75 % 3 = 0 and 75 % 10 = 5, so the output is YES.

Q: Exercise 3: Grocery Mart discounts: total bill 1000 — 10%, 2500 — 20%, 5000 — 35%, 10000 — 50%. Write a program that takes the total bill as input and tells how much discount the user has got and what the discounted price is.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
float bill, discount, price, rate;
printf("Enter total bill: ");
scanf("%f", &bill);
if (bill >= 10000)
rate = 50;
else if (bill >= 5000)
rate = 35;
else if (bill >= 2500)
rate = 20;
else if (bill >= 1000)
rate = 10;
else
rate = 0;
discount = bill * rate / 100;
price = bill - discount;
printf("Discount = %f\n", discount);
printf("Discounted price = %f", price);
getch();
}
Explanation: The nested if-else ladder checks the bill from the highest slab downwards and selects the discount rate: 50% for a bill of 10000 or more, 35% for 5000 or more, 20% for 2500 or more and 10% for 1000 or more; below 1000 there is no discount. The discount amount is bill x rate / 100, and the discounted price is bill minus discount. Example: for a bill of 5000, discount = 1750 and the price to pay is 3250.

Q: Exercise 4: Write a program that takes the original price and sale price of a product as input and tells whether the product is sold on profit or loss. The program should also tell the profit/loss percentage.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
float op, sp, diff, per;
printf("Enter original price: ");
scanf("%f", &op);
printf("Enter sale price: ");
scanf("%f", &sp);
if (sp > op)
{
diff = sp - op;
per = diff / op * 100;
printf("Profit = %f, Profit percentage = %f", diff, per);
}
else if (sp < op)
{
diff = op - sp;
per = diff / op * 100;
printf("Loss = %f, Loss percentage = %f", diff, per);
}
else
printf("No profit, no loss");
getch();
}
Explanation: If the sale price is greater than the original price, the difference is profit; if it is smaller, the difference is loss; if both are equal, there is neither profit nor loss. In both cases the percentage is calculated on the original price: percentage = difference / original price x 100. Example: original price 500, sale price 600 gives profit 100 and profit percentage 20%.

Q: Exercise 5: Write a program that takes the lengths of 3 sides of a triangle as input and tells whether it is a right-angled triangle or not. For a right-angled triangle, hypotenuse^2 = base^2 + height^2.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
float a, b, c;
printf("Enter three sides of the triangle: ");
scanf("%f %f %f", &a, &b, &c);
if (a * a == b * b + c * c || b * b == a * a + c * c || c * c == a * a + b * b)
printf("It is a right-angled triangle");
else
printf("It is not a right-angled triangle");
getch();
}
Explanation: In a right-angled triangle, the square of the longest side (hypotenuse) equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides. Because any of the three sides can be the hypotenuse, all three possibilities are checked and joined with the OR operator ||: if even one of them holds, the triangle is right-angled. Example: sides 3, 4, 5 give 25 = 9 + 16, so it is a right-angled triangle.

Q: Exercise 6: Eligibility for admission in an IT University: at least 60% marks in Matric, at least 65% marks in Intermediate (Pre-Engineering or ICS), at least 65% marks in entrance test. Write a program that takes the obtained and total marks of Matric, Intermediate and Entrance Test as input and tells whether the student is eligible or not.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
float mo, mt, io, it, eo, et, pm, pi, pe;
printf("Enter Matric obtained and total marks: ");
scanf("%f %f", &mo, &mt);
printf("Enter Intermediate obtained and total marks: ");
scanf("%f %f", &io, &it);
printf("Enter Entrance Test obtained and total marks: ");
scanf("%f %f", &eo, &et);
pm = mo / mt * 100;
pi = io / it * 100;
pe = eo / et * 100;
if (pm >= 60 && pi >= 65 && pe >= 65)
printf("The student is eligible for admission");
else
printf("The student is not eligible for admission");
getch();
}
Explanation: The program first converts the obtained marks into percentages: percentage = obtained / total x 100, for Matric (pm), Intermediate (pi) and the entrance test (pe). All three conditions of the university must be satisfied together, so they are joined with the AND operator &&: Matric at least 60%, Intermediate at least 65% and entrance test at least 65%. If even one percentage is below its limit, the student is declared not eligible.

Q: Exercise 7: Bonus table — (Salary 10000, Experience 2 years, Bonus Tasks 5, Bonus 1500); (10000, 3 years, 10 tasks, 2500); (25000, 3 years, 4 tasks, 2000); (75000, 4 years, 7 tasks, 3500); (100000, 5 years, 10 tasks, 5000). Write a program that takes salary, experience and number of bonus tasks of an employee as input and displays the bonus.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int salary, exp, tasks, bonus;
printf("Enter salary: ");
scanf("%d", &salary);
printf("Enter experience in years: ");
scanf("%d", &exp);
printf("Enter number of bonus tasks: ");
scanf("%d", &tasks);
if (salary == 10000 && exp == 2 && tasks == 5)
bonus = 1500;
else if (salary == 10000 && exp == 3 && tasks == 10)
bonus = 2500;
else if (salary == 25000 && exp == 3 && tasks == 4)
bonus = 2000;
else if (salary == 75000 && exp == 4 && tasks == 7)
bonus = 3500;
else if (salary == 100000 && exp == 5 && tasks == 10)
bonus = 5000;
else
bonus = 0;
printf("Bonus = %d", bonus);
getch();
}
Explanation: Each row of the table is one combination of salary, experience and bonus tasks, so every step of the if-else ladder checks all three values together with the AND operator &&. When a complete combination matches a row of the table, the bonus of that row is selected. If no row matches, the bonus is 0. Example: salary 25000, experience 3 years and 4 tasks match the third row, so the bonus displayed is 2000.

lessons.title: Define the following terms
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) Data Structure

A data structure is a way of organizing and storing data in the memory of a computer so that it can be used easily and efficiently. An array is a data structure: it stores many values of the same type together under one name.

Q: 2) Array

An array is a data structure that stores a fixed number of values of the same data type in contiguous (continuous) memory locations under a single name. Each value, called an element, is referred to by its index (position), which starts from 0. For example, int marks[5]; creates an array of 5 integers.

Q: 3) Array Initialization

Array initialization means giving starting values to the elements of an array. It can be done at the time of declaration in a single statement by writing the values in braces, for example int a[5] = {2, 4, 6, 8, 10}; or later, one element at a time, for example a[0] = 2; a[1] = 4;.

Q: 4) Loop Structure

A loop structure is a control structure that repeats a set of instructions again and again until a given condition is satisfied. It saves the programmer from writing the same statements many times. The for loop is a loop structure; it has three parts: initialization, condition and increment/decrement.

Q: 5) Nested Loops

When one loop is written inside the body of another loop, the structure is called nested loops. The outer loop runs its body, and for every single run of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely. Nested loops are used for patterns, tables and two-dimensional data.

lessons.title: Briefly answer the following questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) Is loop a data structure? Justify your answer.

No, a loop is not a data structure. A data structure is a way of storing and organizing data in memory, for example an array stores values. A loop is a control structure: it does not store any data; it only controls the flow of the program by repeating a set of instructions. Loops are often used with data structures (for example, to read or print all elements of an array), but using a data structure does not make the loop itself a data structure.

Q: 2) What is the use of nested loops?

Nested loops are used when a task has to be repeated in rows and columns, or when one repetition depends on another. Their common uses are: printing patterns of stars, numbers and characters; printing multiplication tables for many numbers; working with arrays inside arrays (two-dimensional data); and finding results such as factorials of a whole range of numbers. In a nested loop, the inner loop completes all its rounds for each single round of the outer loop.

Q: 3) What is the advantage of initializing an array at the time of declaration?

Initializing an array at the time of declaration has three advantages: (1) All values are given in a single statement, so the code is short and clear, for example int a[] = {1, 2, 3};. (2) No element is left with a garbage value, which can happen if values are assigned later and one element is forgotten. (3) If the size is not written, the compiler itself counts the values and fixes the size of the array, so there is no chance of a size mistake.

Q: 4) Describe the structure of a for loop.

Structure of a for loop:
for (initialization; condition; increment/decrement)
{
body of the loop;
}
The initialization part gives the starting value to the loop variable and runs only once, at the beginning. The condition is checked before every round; the body runs only while the condition is satisfied. After each round, the increment/decrement part changes the loop variable (for example i++ increases it by 1). When the condition becomes not satisfied, the loop ends. The three parts in the parentheses are separated by semicolons.

Q: 5) How can you declare an array? Briefly describe the three parts of array declaration.

An array is declared by writing its data type, its name and its size, for example: int marks[5]; The three parts of an array declaration are: (1) Data type — the type of values the array will store, for example int, float or char. (2) Array name — the unique identifier by which the whole array is referred to, for example marks. (3) Array size — the number of elements, written in square brackets, for example [5]. The size tells the compiler how much memory to reserve; the indexes of this array run from 0 to 4.

mcqs.q: A loop is NOT a data structure because a loop:
options: does not store any data; it only controls the flow of the program
mcqs.why: A data structure stores and organizes data in memory, like an array. A loop is a control structure: it stores nothing and only repeats a set of instructions, even though loops are often used with data structures.

mcqs.q: A loop is classified as a:
mcqs.why: A loop is a control structure because it controls the flow of the program by repeating instructions; an array, by contrast, is a data structure.

mcqs.q: Nested loops are commonly used for:
options: printing patterns of stars, numbers and characters
mcqs.why: Nested loops are used when a task repeats in rows and columns: printing patterns, printing multiplication tables for many numbers and working with two-dimensional data.

mcqs.q: One advantage of initializing an array at the time of declaration is:
options: no element is left with a garbage value
mcqs.why: When values are assigned later one by one, an element may be forgotten and left with a garbage value; initializing at declaration gives all values in a single statement, so this cannot happen.

mcqs.q: If the size is not written while initializing an array at declaration, then:
options: the compiler itself counts the values and fixes the size
mcqs.why: For example, int a[] = {1, 2, 3}; the compiler counts the three values and fixes the size as 3, so there is no chance of a size mistake.

mcqs.q: In a for loop, the initialization part runs:
mcqs.why: Initialization gives the starting value to the loop variable and runs only once; the condition is checked before every round and increment/decrement runs after each round.

mcqs.q: In a for loop, the condition is checked:
mcqs.why: The body of the loop runs only while the condition is satisfied; the condition is checked before every round, and when it becomes not satisfied the loop ends.

mcqs.q: An array declaration has how many parts?
mcqs.why: The three parts of an array declaration are: data type, array name and array size, for example int (type), marks (name) and [5] (size) in int marks[5];

mcqs.q: The array int marks[5]; has indexes running from:
mcqs.why: Indexes start from 0, so a 5-element array has indexes 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4; the last index is always size - 1.

mcqs.q: The size written in an array declaration tells the compiler:
mcqs.why: The array size tells the compiler how much memory to reserve for the array; the data type tells the kind of values and the name is the identifier used to refer to the array.

lessons.title: Identify the errors in the following code segments
lessons.notes_html:
Q: a) int a[] = ({2},{3},{4});

Error: The values of the array are written in separate parentheses ( ) and braces are mixed wrongly. In C, all the values of an array are written together inside one pair of curly braces { }, separated by commas. Corrected code: int a[] = {2, 3, 4};

Q: b) for (int i = 0, i < 10, i++) printf("%d ", i);

Error: The three parts of the for loop header are separated by commas. In C, initialization, condition and increment/decrement must be separated by semicolons. Corrected code: for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) printf("%d ", i);

Q: c) int a[] = {1,2,3,4,5}; for (int j = 0; j < 5; j++) printf("%d ", a(j));

Error: The array element is referred to as a(j), using parentheses, as if the array were a function. Array elements are accessed with square brackets [ ] and the index number. Corrected code: printf("%d ", a[j]);

Q: d) float f[] = {1.4, 3.5, 7.3, 5.9}; int size = 4; for (int n = -1; n < size; n--) printf("%f ", f[n]);

Errors: (1) The loop starts with n = -1, but array indexes start from 0; f[-1] is an invalid location outside the array. (2) The update part n-- decreases n further (-2, -3, ...), so the condition n < size always stays satisfied and the loop never ends, reading invalid memory locations. Corrected code (printing in forward order): for (int n = 0; n < size; n++) printf("%f ", f[n]);

Q: e) int count = 0; for (int i = 4; i < 6; i--) for (int j = i, j < 45; j++) { count++; printf("%count", count) }

Errors: (1) In the inner for header, a comma is used after j = i; the parts of a for header are separated by semicolons: for (int j = i; j < 45; j++). (2) The outer loop uses i-- with the condition i < 6: i decreases from 4, so it always remains less than 6 and the loop never ends; it should be i++. (3) The format specifier in printf("%count", count) is wrong; %c would need a character and here an integer is printed, so it must be printf("%d", count);. (4) The closing brace } of the outer loop is missing at the end.

mcqs.q: The error in segment (a) int a[] = ({2},{3},{4}); is that:
options: the array has too many values
the values are written in separate parentheses instead of one pair of curly braces
mcqs.why: All values of an array are written together inside one pair of curly braces { }, separated by commas. Corrected code: int a[] = {2, 3, 4};

mcqs.q: In segment (b) for (int i = 0, i < 10, i++), the three parts of the for header are wrongly separated by:
mcqs.why: Initialization, condition and increment/decrement in a for header must be separated by semicolons: for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++).

mcqs.q: In segment (c), the element is written as a(j). Array elements must be referred to with:
mcqs.why: a(j) treats the array like a function. Array elements are accessed with square brackets and the index number: printf("%d ", a[j]);

mcqs.q: In segment (d), the loop starts with n = -1. This is an error because:
options: loops cannot start from a negative value in any program
array indexes start from 0, so f[-1] is an invalid location outside the array
mcqs.why: Array indexes start from 0, so f[-1] refers to a location outside the array, which is invalid; the loop should start from n = 0.

mcqs.q: In segment (d), the update n-- with the condition n < size makes the loop:
options: never end, reading invalid memory locations
mcqs.why: n decreases further (-2, -3, ...), so the condition n < size always stays satisfied and the loop never ends. The corrected loop uses n++ starting from 0.

mcqs.q: In segment (e), the inner for header is written for (int j = i, j < 45; j++). The error is:
options: a comma is used after j = i instead of a semicolon
mcqs.why: The parts of a for header are separated by semicolons, so it must be: for (int j = i; j < 45; j++).

mcqs.q: In segment (e), the outer loop uses i-- with the condition i < 6, starting from i = 4. The result is:
options: the loop never ends because i always remains less than 6
mcqs.why: With i--, i decreases from 4 and always remains less than 6, so the condition never becomes false; it should be i++ so that i can reach 6 and end the loop.

mcqs.q: In segment (e), printf("%count", count) is wrong because:
options: count is an integer and the format specifier is wrong; it must be %d
mcqs.why: %count is not a valid format specifier for an integer (%c would need a character); the correct statement is printf("%d", count);

mcqs.q: One more error in segment (e) is that:
options: the closing brace } of the outer loop is missing at the end
mcqs.why: The book lists four errors in segment (e): the comma in the inner header, i-- making the loop endless, the wrong format specifier, and the missing closing brace of the outer loop.

mcqs.q: The corrected form of segment (a) is:
mcqs.why: All the values of an array are written together inside one pair of curly braces, separated by commas: int a[] = {2, 3, 4};

Q: b) int i; for (i = 34; i <= 60; i = i * 2) printf("* ");

Working: In the first round i = 34, which is less than or equal to 60, so one star is printed. Then i becomes 34 * 2 = 68, which is greater than 60, so the loop ends. Output: * (a single star)

Q: c) for (int i = 50; i <= 50; i++) { for (j = i; j >= 48; j--) printf("j = %d ", j); printf("i = %d ", i); }

Working: The outer loop runs only once, for i = 50, because after i++ the value 51 fails the condition i <= 50. In that one round, the inner loop runs for j = 50, 49 and 48 and prints the value of j on a new line each time. Then i is printed. Output:
j = 50
j = 49
j = 48
i = 50

Q: d) int i, arr[] = {2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8}; for (i = 0; i < 7; i++) { printf("%d ", arr[i] * arr[i]); i++; }

Working: There is an extra i++ inside the body, so i increases twice in every round and only the elements at even indexes 0, 2, 4 and 6 are used. Their squares are printed: arr[0] x arr[0] = 2 x 2 = 4; arr[2] x arr[2] = 4 x 4 = 16; arr[4] x arr[4] = 6 x 6 = 36; arr[6] x arr[6] = 8 x 8 = 64. When i becomes 7 the loop ends. Output (each on a new line): 4, 16, 36, 64

Q: e) float ar1[] = {1.1, 1.2, 1.3}; float ar2[] = {2.1, 2.2, 2.3}; for (i = 0; i < 3; i++) for (j = i; j < 3; j++) printf("%f ", ar1[i] * ar2[j] * i * j);

Working: The pairs (i, j) that run are (0,0), (0,1), (0,2), (1,1), (1,2) and (2,2). For i = 0, the factor i makes the product 0 in all three rounds, so 0.000000 is printed three times. For (1,1): 1.2 x 2.2 x 1 x 1 = 2.640000. For (1,2): 1.2 x 2.3 x 1 x 2 = 5.520000. For (2,2): 1.3 x 2.3 x 2 x 2 = 11.960000. Output (each on a new line): 0.000000, 0.000000, 0.000000, 2.640000, 5.520000, 11.960000
