Q: Exercise 1(a): Use loops to print the pattern of three rows of five stars each (***** / ***** / *****).

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int i, j;
for (i = 1; i <= 3; i++)
{
for (j = 1; j <= 5; j++)
printf("*");
printf(" ");
}
getch();
}
Explanation: Nested loops are used. The outer loop (i) runs 3 times, once for each row. The inner loop (j) runs 5 times in every row and prints five stars side by side. After each row, printf(" ") moves the cursor to a new line, so the next row of stars starts below the previous one.

Q: Exercise 1(b): Use loops to print the letter pattern: A / BC / DEF / GHIJ / KLMN (letters increase by one in every row).

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int i, j;
char ch = 'A';
for (i = 1; i <= 5; i++)
{
for (j = 1; j <= i; j++)
{
printf("%c", ch);
ch++;
}
printf(" ");
}
getch();
}
Explanation: A char variable ch starts from 'A'. The outer loop runs 5 times for the 5 rows. In row number i, the inner loop runs i times, so row 1 prints 1 letter, row 2 prints 2 letters, and so on. After printing a letter, ch++ moves to the next letter of the alphabet, so the letters continue across rows: A, then B C, then D E F, then G H I J, then K L M N O. Note: the pattern printed in the book shows only four letters (KLMN) in the last row; by the pattern's own rule the fifth row has five letters, KLMNO.

Q: Exercise 2: Write a program that takes two positive integers a and b as input and displays the value of a raised to the power b.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int a, b, i, power = 1;
printf("Enter base a: ");
scanf("%d", &a);
printf("Enter exponent b: ");
scanf("%d", &b);
for (i = 1; i <= b; i++)
power = power * a;
printf("%d raised to power %d = %d", a, b, power);
getch();
}
Explanation: The power of a number means multiplying it by itself repeatedly: a raised to b = a x a x ... (b times). The variable power starts from 1, and the loop multiplies it by a exactly b times. Example: for a = 2 and b = 5, the loop gives 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32.

Q: Exercise 3: Write a program that takes two numbers as input and displays their Greatest Common Divisor (GCD) using the Euclidean method.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int a, b, r;
printf("Enter two numbers: ");
scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);
while (b != 0)
{
r = a % b;
a = b;
b = r;
}
printf("GCD = %d", a);
getch();
}
Explanation: In the Euclidean method, the larger number is repeatedly replaced by the remainder of the division. In each round, r = a % b stores the remainder, then a takes the value of b and b takes the value of r. The loop continues until the remainder becomes 0; at that point the value in a is the GCD. Example: for 48 and 18: 48 % 18 = 12, 18 % 12 = 6, 12 % 6 = 0, so the GCD is 6.

Q: Exercise 4: Write a program to display factorials of numbers from 1 to 7. (Hint: Use nested loops)

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int n, i;
long fact;
for (n = 1; n <= 7; n++)
{
fact = 1;
for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
fact = fact * i;
printf("Factorial of %d = %ld ", n, fact);
}
getch();
}
Explanation: Nested loops are used. The outer loop selects the number n from 1 to 7. For each n, fact is reset to 1 and the inner loop multiplies fact by every number from 1 to n, which is exactly the factorial of n. The results printed are: 1, 2, 6, 24, 120, 720 and 5040.

Q: Exercise 5: Write a program that takes 10 numbers as input in an array and displays the product of the first and last element on the console.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int a[10], i, product;
printf("Enter 10 numbers: ");
for (i = 0; i < 10; i++)
scanf("%d", &a[i]);
product = a[0] * a[9];
printf("Product of first and last element = %d", product);
getch();
}
Explanation: A loop is used to read the 10 numbers into the array a, which is the easy way to fill an array. The first element is at index 0, that is a[0], and the last (tenth) element is at index 9, that is a[9], because array indexes start from 0. The two are multiplied and the product is displayed.

Q: Exercise 6: Write a program that declares and initializes an array of 7 elements and tells how many elements in the array are greater than 10.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void main()
{
int a[7] = {4, 15, 8, 22, 10, 35, 7};
int i, count = 0;
for (i = 0; i < 7; i++)
{
if (a[i] > 10)
count++;
}
printf("Elements greater than 10 = %d", count);
getch();
}
Explanation: The array is declared and initialized in a single statement with 7 elements. A loop visits every element one by one; whenever an element is greater than 10, the counter count is increased by 1. In this array, 15, 22 and 35 are greater than 10, so the program displays 3. The same program works for any values placed in the array.

lessons.title: Define the following
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) Functions

A function is a block of statements that performs a particular task. A program is divided into functions so that each function does one specific job, for example calculating a square or printing a table. The main() is also a function; execution starts from it, and it calls other functions when their task is needed.

Q: 2) Built-in functions

Built-in functions are the functions that are already available in the C Standard Library; the programmer does not write them, he only uses (calls) them. Examples are printf() and scanf() from stdio.h and getch() from conio.h. The functions a programmer writes himself are called user-defined functions.

Q: 3) Function Parameters

Parameters are the variables written in the parentheses of a function definition, which receive the values passed to the function when it is called. For example, in int square(int x), x is a parameter. The values actually passed in the call, for example square(5), are called arguments; the parameter x receives the argument 5.

Q: 4) Reusability

Reusability means that a piece of code written once can be used again and again, in the same program and in other programs, without writing it again. Functions give reusability: once a function is defined, it can be called any number of times from any part of the program, which saves time and effort.

Q: 5) Calling a function

Calling a function means transferring the control of the program to that function so that its statements are executed. A function is called by writing its name with the required arguments in parentheses, for example sum = square(5);. When the function finishes its work, control returns to the point from where it was called, along with the returned value if any.

lessons.title: Briefly answer the following questions
lessons.notes_html:
Q: 1) What is the difference between arguments and parameters? Give an example.

Parameters are the variables declared in the function definition, which act as placeholders to receive values. Arguments are the actual values passed to the function when it is called. Example: in the definition int square(int x), x is a parameter. In the call square(6), the value 6 is an argument; it is copied into the parameter x, and the function returns 36. In short: parameters belong to the definition, arguments belong to the call.

Q: 2) Enlist the parts of a function definition.

A function definition has the following parts: (1) Return type — the data type of the value the function sends back, for example int; void is used when nothing is returned. (2) Function name — a meaningful name related to its task, for example square. (3) Parameters — the list of input variables in parentheses, with their data types. Together, return type, name and parameters make the function signature (header). (4) Body of the function — the set of statements written inside { } that actually perform the task, including the return statement when a value is sent back.

Q: 3) Is it necessary to use compatible data types in function definition and function call? Justify your answer with an example.

Yes, it is necessary. The arguments passed in a call are copied into the parameters of the definition, so their data types must match (be compatible); otherwise the value can be changed or lost, or the compiler gives an error. Example: if a function is defined as int square(int x) and it is called as square(4.5), the argument 4.5 does not fit in the int parameter x; it is cut down to 4, and the function returns 16 instead of 20.25. The answer is wrong only because the data types were not compatible. In the same way, the type of the returned value must match the variable that receives it.

Q: 4) Describe the advantages of using functions.

The advantages of using functions are: (1) Reusability of code — a function is written once and can be called many times, so the same code is not written again and again. (2) Separation of tasks — the program is divided into small parts, each doing one clear task, which keeps the program organized. (3) Reduction in complexity — a large problem is broken into small, simple problems that are easy to solve one by one. (4) Readability — the program becomes easy to read and understand, because main() shows the overall plan and details stay inside functions. (5) Easy debugging — if an error occurs, only the concerned function has to be checked and corrected.

Q: 5) What do you know about the return keyword?

The return keyword is used inside a function to send a value back to the part of the program that called the function, and to transfer control back at the same time. As soon as return is executed, the function ends, even if more statements are written after it — that is why, when a function body has three return statements (for example in different if blocks), only one of them is executed in a single call. The type of the value returned must match the return type written in the function header; a function with void return type cannot return a value. Example: return x * x; in the square function sends the square back to the caller.

mcqs.why: Return type, name and parameters together make the function signature, also called the header; the statements that perform the task form the body.

options: the argument 4.5 is cut down to 4 in the int parameter
the compiler gives an error and stops
mcqs.why: The argument is copied into an int parameter, so 4.5 does not fit and is cut down to 4; the function then returns 4 * 4 = 16 instead of 20.25. Data types in the definition and the call must be compatible.

options: the whole program must be rewritten
only the concerned function has to be checked and corrected
the compiler removes the error itself
the program is divided into arrays
mcqs.why: Because the program is divided into small functions, each doing one task, an error can be located in one function and corrected there.

mcqs.why: Dividing the program into small parts, each doing one clear task, keeps the program organized and reduces its complexity.

options: transfers control back to the caller
mcqs.why: As soon as return is executed, the function ends and control transfers back to the calling part of the program, even if more statements are written after it.

mcqs.why: The type of the returned value must match the return type in the header; a void function returns nothing, so writing return 23; in it is an error.

mcqs.why: Writing the function name with an argument calls the function; the value it returns is then stored in s by the assignment operator.

lessons.title: Identify the errors in the following code segments
lessons.notes_html:
Q: a) void sum (int a, int b) { return a + b; }

Error: The function is declared with the return type void, which means it returns nothing, yet its body contains return a + b;, which tries to return a value. Correction: change the return type to the type of the value being returned: int sum (int a, int b) { return a + b; }

Q: b) void message (); { printf("Hope you are fine :)"); return 23; }

Errors: (1) A semicolon is written after the function header void message (); — this makes it a function declaration (prototype), so the following block { } does not belong to any function and causes an error. The semicolon must be removed. (2) The function is void (returns nothing) but its body contains return 23;, which returns a value; this statement must be removed (or the return type changed to int). Corrected code: void message () { printf("Hope you are fine :)"); }

Q: c) int max (int a; int b) { if (a > b) return a; return b; }

Error: The two parameters in the function header are separated by a semicolon: (int a; int b). Parameters in a function definition are always separated by a comma. Corrected code: int max (int a, int b) { if (a > b) return a; return b; }

Q: d) int product (int n1, int n2) return n1 * n2;

Error: The body of the function is not enclosed in curly braces { }. Every function definition must have its statements inside a block. Corrected code: int product (int n1, int n2) { return n1 * n2; }

Q: e) int totalDigits (int x) { int count = 0; for (int i = x; i >= 1, i = i / 10) count++; return count };

Errors: (1) In the for header, a comma is written between the condition and the update part: i >= 1, i = i / 10 — the three parts of a for header are separated by semicolons, so it must be for (int i = x; i >= 1; i = i / 10). With the comma, the loop has no proper update and does not work as intended. (2) The statement return count has no semicolon at its end; it must be return count;. (3) An extra }; is written at the end: a function definition closes with } only, without a semicolon. Corrected code: int totalDigits (int x) { int count = 0; for (int i = x; i >= 1; i = i / 10) count++; return count; }

mcqs.q: The error in segment (a) void sum (int a, int b) { return a + b; } is that:
options: a void function returns nothing, yet the body tries to return a value
the function name is a reserved word
mcqs.why: void means the function returns nothing, but return a + b; tries to return the sum. Correction: change the return type to int sum (int a, int b).

mcqs.q: The correct way to fix segment (a) is to:
options: change the return type from void to int
remove the return statement and print nothing
add a semicolon after the header
mcqs.why: The return type must match the type of the value being returned; the sum of two ints is an int, so the header becomes int sum (int a, int b).

mcqs.q: In segment (b), the semicolon written after the header void message (); makes it:
options: a function declaration (prototype), so the following block belongs to no function
mcqs.why: A semicolon after a function header turns it into a declaration; the block { } that follows then belongs to no function and causes an error. The semicolon must be removed.

mcqs.q: Segment (b) also contains return 23; inside the void function message. This statement must be:
options: removed (or the return type changed to int)
mcqs.why: A void function cannot return a value, so return 23; is an error; the corrected function only prints the message.

mcqs.q: In segment (c) int max (int a; int b), the parameters are separated by a semicolon. Parameters must be separated by:
mcqs.why: Parameters in a function definition are always separated by a comma: int max (int a, int b).

mcqs.q: The error in segment (d) int product (int n1, int n2) return n1 * n2; is that:
options: the body of the function is not enclosed in curly braces { }
mcqs.why: Every function definition must have its statements inside a block: int product (int n1, int n2) { return n1 * n2; }

mcqs.q: In segment (e), a comma is written between the condition and the update part of the for header. The parts of a for header are separated by:
mcqs.why: It must be written as for (int i = x; i >= 1; i = i / 10). With the comma, the loop has no proper update part and does not work as intended.

mcqs.q: In segment (e), the statement return count has no semicolon at its end. This causes:
mcqs.why: Every statement in C must end with the statement terminator; the statement must be written as return count;

mcqs.q: Segment (e) ends with an extra }; after the function. A function definition closes with:
mcqs.why: Unlike a structure declaration, a function definition closes with } only; the extra semicolon after it is an error.

mcqs.q: The function totalDigits in segment (e) counts the digits of a number by repeatedly:
mcqs.why: The loop update i = i / 10 removes one digit in every round, and count++ counts the rounds, so count becomes the total number of digits.

lessons.title: Write down output of the following code segments
lessons.notes_html:
Q: a) int xyz (int n) { return n + n; } int main() { int p = xyx(5); p = xyz(p); printf("%d ", p); } [function names as printed in the book]

Note on the printed code: main() calls xyx(5), but the function defined in the segment is named xyz; xyx is not defined anywhere, so as printed the program gives an error and does not run. Taking xyx as a printing mistake for xyz, the working is: p = xyz(5) returns 5 + 5 = 10, so p becomes 10. Then p = xyz(p) = xyz(10) returns 10 + 10 = 20. Output: 20

Q: b) void abc (int a, int b, int c) { int sum = a + b + c; } int main() { int x = 4, y = 7, z = 23, sum1 = 0; abc (x, y, z); printf("%d %d %d", x, y, z); } [commas in printf as required by C syntax]

Working: The function abc receives copies of x, y and z and adds them into its own local variable sum (4 + 7 + 23 = 34). But sum is local to abc and the function is void, so nothing is sent back; the variables x, y and z in main are not changed at all (and sum1 is never printed). Output: 4 7 23

Q: c) int aa (int x) { int p = x / 10; x++; p = p + (p * x); return p; } int main() { printf("We got %d ", aa(aa(23))); }

Working: First the inner call aa(23) is solved: p = 23 / 10 = 2 (integer division); x++ makes x = 24; p = p + (p * x) = 2 + (2 x 24) = 2 + 48 = 50. So the inner call returns 50. Now the outer call aa(50): p = 50 / 10 = 5; x++ makes x = 51; p = 5 + (5 x 51) = 5 + 255 = 260. Output: We got 260

Q: d) float f3 (int n1, int n2) { n1 = n1 + n2; n2 = n2 - n1; return 0; } int main() { printf("%f\n", f3(3, 2)); printf("%f\n", f3(10, 6)); }

Working: Whatever values are passed, the function f3 always ends with return 0;, so every call returns 0. In the first call f3(3, 2): n1 becomes 5 and n2 becomes 2 - 5 = -3, but these are not returned; the returned value is 0, printed with %f as 0.000000. The second call f3(10, 6) also returns 0. Output (each on a new line): 0.000000 and 0.000000

mcqs.q: As printed, segment (a) calls xyx(5), but the function defined is named xyz. As printed, the program:
options: gives an error because xyx is not defined anywhere
mcqs.why: The book itself notes this misprint: main() calls xyx(5), but only xyz is defined, so as printed the program gives an error and does not run.

mcqs.q: Taking xyx in segment (a) as a printing mistake for xyz, the output is:
mcqs.why: Working: xyz(n) returns n + n. p = xyz(5) = 10, then p = xyz(p) = xyz(10) = 20. Output: 20.

mcqs.q: The output of segment (b) — abc(x, y, z) with x = 4, y = 7, z = 23, then printing x, y, z — is:
mcqs.why: Working: abc receives copies of the values and adds them into its own local variable sum, but it is a void function and returns nothing, so x, y and z in main are unchanged. Output: 4 7 23.

mcqs.q: In segment (b), the sum 34 calculated inside abc is not available in main() because:
options: sum is a local variable of abc and nothing is returned
mcqs.why: sum is declared inside abc, so it exists only within that function; abc is void and returns no value, and the variable sum1 in main is never printed.

mcqs.q: In segment (c), the inner call aa(23) returns:
mcqs.why: Working: in aa(23), p = 23 / 10 = 2 (integer division); x++ makes x = 24; p = p + (p * x) = 2 + (2 * 24) = 50. So the inner call returns 50.

mcqs.q: The output of segment (c) — printf("We got %d ", aa(aa(23))); — is:
mcqs.why: Working: the inner call aa(23) returns 50. The outer call aa(50): p = 50 / 10 = 5; x++ makes x = 51; p = 5 + (5 * 51) = 260. Output: We got 260.

mcqs.q: In segment (d), the function f3 always ends with return 0; so the first call f3(3, 2) returns:
mcqs.why: Working: inside the call, n1 becomes 5 and n2 becomes -3, but these are not returned; the function always executes return 0;, so every call returns 0.

mcqs.q: Both values printed by segment (d) are:
mcqs.why: Working: both calls return 0, and because the values are printed with %f, each is displayed in float form as 0.000000 on its own line.

mcqs.q: In segment (c), in the computation for aa(23), after x++ the value of x used in p + (p * x) is:
mcqs.why: Working: x starts as 23; x++ increases it to 24 before p = p + (p * x) is calculated, so p = 2 + (2 * 24) = 50.

mcqs.q: In segment (b), the variables x, y and z in main() are not changed by the call abc(x, y, z) because:
options: the function receives copies of the values, not the variables themselves
mcqs.why: Arguments are copied into the parameters of the function; changes inside the function affect only the copies, so the original variables in main() keep their values 4, 7 and 23.

lessons.title: Programming Exercises
lessons.notes_html:
Q: Exercise 1: Write a function int square(int x); to calculate the square of an integer x.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
int square (int x)
{
return x * x;
}
void main()
{
int n, s;
printf("Enter a number: ");
scanf("%d", &n);
s = square(n);
printf("Square of %d = %d", n, s);
getch();
}
Line-by-line explanation: The header file stdio.h is included for printf/scanf and conio.h for getch(). The function square is defined with return type int and one int parameter x. Inside it, return x * x; calculates the square and sends it back to the caller. In main, a number is read into n. The statement s = square(n); calls the function: the value of n is passed as the argument, and the returned square is stored in s. Finally printf displays the result. Example: for n = 6, the output is Square of 6 = 36.

Q: Exercise 2: Write a function int power(int x, int y); to calculate and return x raised to the power y.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
int power (int x, int y)
{
int p = 1, i;
for (i = 1; i <= y; i++)
p = p * x;
return p;
}
void main()
{
int a, b, ans;
printf("Enter base and exponent: ");
scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);
ans = power(a, b);
printf("%d raised to power %d = %d", a, b, ans);
getch();
}
Line-by-line explanation: The function power takes two parameters: the base x and the exponent y. The variable p starts from 1. The for loop runs y times, and in every round p is multiplied by x, so after y rounds p holds x multiplied by itself y times, that is, x raised to the power y. The return statement sends p back. In main, the base and exponent are read, the function is called, and the returned answer is printed. Example: power(2, 5) returns 32.

Q: Exercise 3: Write a function to calculate the factorial of a number.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
long factorial (int n)
{
long f = 1;
int i;
for (i = 1; i <= n; i++)
f = f * i;
return f;
}
void main()
{
int n;
printf("Enter a number: ");
scanf("%d", &n);
printf("Factorial of %d = %ld", n, factorial(n));
getch();
}
Line-by-line explanation: The function factorial receives the number n as its parameter. The variable f (long, because factorials grow quickly) starts from 1. The loop runs from 1 to n and multiplies f by every number in turn, so f becomes 1 x 2 x ... x n, which is the factorial of n. The value is returned and printed by main. Example: factorial(5) = 1 x 2 x 3 x 4 x 5 = 120.

Q: Exercise 4: Write a function which takes values for three angles of a triangle and prints whether the given values make a valid triangle or not. A valid triangle is the one where the sum of the three angles is equal to 180.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void checkTriangle (int a, int b, int c)
{
if (a + b + c == 180 && a > 0 && b > 0 && c > 0)
printf("The angles make a valid triangle");
else
printf("The angles do not make a valid triangle");
}
void main()
{
int x, y, z;
printf("Enter three angles: ");
scanf("%d %d %d", &x, &y, &z);
checkTriangle(x, y, z);
getch();
}
Line-by-line explanation: The function checkTriangle receives the three angles as parameters a, b and c. Its return type is void because it only prints a message and returns no value. The if condition checks two things joined by &&: the sum of the angles must be exactly 180, and every angle must be greater than 0. If both hold, the valid message is printed; otherwise the else part prints the not-valid message. Example: angles 60, 60, 60 sum to 180, so the triangle is valid.

Q: Exercise 5: Write a function which takes the amount and the interest percentage and returns the interest amount.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
float interest (float amount, float per)
{
return amount * per / 100;
}
void main()
{
float amt, p, ins;
printf("Enter amount: ");
scanf("%f", &amt);
printf("Enter interest percentage: ");
scanf("%f", &p);
ins = interest(amt, p);
printf("Interest amount = %f", ins);
getch();
}
Line-by-line explanation: The function interest takes two float parameters: the amount and the interest percentage. Inside, it applies the formula interest = amount x percentage / 100 and returns the result, which is a float, matching the float return type in the header. In main, the amount and percentage are read from the user, the function is called, and the returned interest amount is stored in ins and displayed. Example: amount 20000 at 10% gives interest 2000.

Q: Exercise 6: Write a function which takes a number as input and displays its digits with spaces in between.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void showDigits (int n)
{
int d = 1, digit;
while (n / d >= 10)
d = d * 10;
while (d >= 1)
{
digit = n / d;
printf("%d ", digit);
n = n % d;
d = d / 10;
}
}
void main()
{
int num;
printf("Enter a number: ");
scanf("%d", &num);
showDigits(num);
getch();
}
Line-by-line explanation: The function showDigits receives the number n. First, the variable d is raised to the place value of the first (leftmost) digit: for 2534, d becomes 1000. Then, in the second loop, digit = n / d picks the leftmost digit and prints it followed by a space; n = n % d removes that digit from the number; and d = d / 10 moves to the next lower place. This repeats until all digits are printed. For 2534 the display is: 2 5 3 4.

Q: Exercise 7: Write a function to print the table of a number.

Program:
#include <stdio.h>
#include <conio.h>
void table (int n)
{
int i;
for (i = 1; i <= 10; i++)
printf("%d x %d = %d\n", n, i, n * i);
}
void main()
{
int num;
printf("Enter a number: ");
scanf("%d", &num);
table(num);
getch();
}
Line-by-line explanation: The function table receives the number n whose table is to be printed; it is void because it only prints and returns nothing. The for loop runs i from 1 to 10. In every round, printf prints one line of the table in the form n x i = n*i, and the \n at the end takes each line to a new row. In main, the number is read from the user and passed to the function. Example: table(4) prints 4 x 1 = 4 up to 4 x 10 = 40.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 1, the function square is called with n = 6. The output printed is:
mcqs.why: Working: s = square(6) returns 6 * 6 = 36, and printf displays: Square of 6 = 36.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 2, the value returned by power(2, 5) is:
mcqs.why: Working: the loop in power runs y = 5 times, multiplying p by x = 2 each time: 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 32.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 3, the value of factorial(5) is:
mcqs.why: Working: factorial multiplies f by every number from 1 to n: 1 x 2 x 3 x 4 x 5 = 120.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 3, the return type of the factorial function is long because:
options: factorials grow quickly and become large
mcqs.why: Factorials grow very fast (7! = 5040 and larger numbers grow even faster), so the variable f and the return type are long to hold the bigger values.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 4, checkTriangle has the return type void because it:
options: only prints a message and returns no value
mcqs.why: checkTriangle receives the three angles and only prints whether the triangle is valid; since it sends no value back, its return type is void.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 4, the angles 60, 60, 60 make a valid triangle because:
options: their sum is exactly 180 and every angle is greater than 0
mcqs.why: Working: 60 + 60 + 60 = 180, and all three angles are greater than 0, so both parts of the condition joined by && are satisfied and the valid message is printed.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 5, the interest on an amount of 20000 at 10% returned by the interest function is:
mcqs.why: Working: interest = amount x percentage / 100 = 20000 x 10 / 100 = 2000, returned as a float by the function.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 6, the function showDigits(2534) displays:
mcqs.why: Working: d is raised to 1000, the place value of the first digit; each round prints n / d (the leftmost digit) with a space, removes it with n % d and divides d by 10. Display: 2 5 3 4.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 7, the last line printed by table(4) is:
mcqs.why: Working: the loop in table runs i from 1 to 10, printing n x i = n * i in each round; the last round is i = 10, which prints 4 x 10 = 40.

mcqs.q: In Exercise 2, the loop inside the power function runs exactly:
mcqs.why: The for loop runs from i = 1 to y, so p is multiplied by x exactly y times, giving x raised to the power y.
